TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
THURSDAY, 23 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
DAY 35
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR ALEXANDER VIAL, for the Commonwealth
MR MICHAEL PRUSCINO, for the Commonwealth
MS FIONA McLEOD AO KC, for Mr Finn Pratt
MS LINDY BARRETT, for Mr Finn Pratt
MR MATTHEW BRADY KC, for Ms Serena Wilson

COMMISSIONER: Right. Some appearances, please.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. If it please the Commission, I appear with Ms Marsh this morning.
COMMISSIONER: Ms Hogan-Doran, you have got Mr Vial?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: May it please the Commission, I appear today with Mr Vial and
Mr Pruscino for the Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms McLeod?
MS McLEOD: Good morning, Commissioner. I appear for Mr Pratt, with Ms Barrett of
Counsel.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And Mr Brady?
MR BRADY: Yes. Good morning, Commissioner. With the Commission's leave, I appear for the
witness this morning, Ms Serena Wilson.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Now, I think Ms Wilson was excused on the last occasion and
may need to be re-sworn.
MR GREGGERY: That's correct.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. I will have to get to you take an oath or an affirmation again,
Ms Wilson. I can't remember which you took last time.
MS WILSON: Affirmation.
COMMISSIONER: Affirmation. Thanks. Would you mind standing?
<SERENA WILSON, AFFIRMED
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Mr Greggery.
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY
MR GREGGERY: Yes, Commissioner. Perhaps before I start with Ms Wilson, I might tender the
exhibits. They commence on the draft, in terms of new exhibits, at number 5664 and
conclude at number 5731.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Well, the exhibits listed - the items listed on the draft which
haven't previously been admitted are now admitted with the numbers they bear in the draft
exhibit list. Thank you.

<EXHIBITS 5664 TO 5731 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY
MR GREGGERY: Ms Wilson, you provided an additional Statement since you last gave
evidence dated 21 February 2023?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you did that, as I understand that Statement, because you had the
opportunity to reflect upon the evidence that you previously gave and documents which you
say you had not seen prior to giving evidence?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: There are some typographical errors of a minor nature in respect of that
document. Do you have a copy in front of you?
MS WILSON: I do.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. Perhaps if you could take us to those.
MS WILSON: Yes. Paragraph 10 on page 2.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: The second sentence - this is an editing rather than a typographical - should
commence:
As far as I am aware, DSS did not see the final Executive Minute in 2015 before it went to the
Minister and were not included at the table...
Et cetera. And then the final sentence in that paragraph:
No opportunity was given to DSS to scrutinise it before it went to the Minister.
MR GREGGERY: Sorry, what was the last amendment?
MS WILSON:
No opportunity was given to DSS to scrutinise it...
That is, the Executive Minute:
...before it went to the Minister.

MS WILSON: Page 3, paragraph 12.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: The second sentence should start:
It is my belief that it was only after the OCI was implemented so badly and the Ombudsman's
own-motion inquiry commenced that DHS engaged with DSS. And even then, it was quite
superficial.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you.
MS WILSON: Page 4, paragraph 23. There's a missing "of" in the final - second-last sentence:
...because of the information that DHS had procedural guidelines.
And page 5, paragraph 29, there's a redundant "for" in the first sentence. So it should read:
On 24 February 2017, the Ombudsman's Office subsequently requested advice.
Deleting the "for".
MR GREGGERY: Thank you.
MS WILSON: And I believe that's it, Counsel.
MR GREGGERY: One of the topics that you cover in that Statement, Ms Wilson, is - in broad
terms is the question of whether you were aware that averaging was being used by DHS
under the PAYG Manual Compliance Scheme and the OCI Scheme prior to the Ombudsman's
investigation in January 2017. Is that right?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And as I understand the effect of your Statement, you say that you were not
aware that averaging was being used?
MS WILSON: That's correct. I was - yes.
MR GREGGERY: Another topic that you address in your Statement is the approach that you
perceived or were aware of by Coalition Ministers in respect of social security which was
different to the previous Government, and that included the Ministers and their staff.
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: From recollection, I think you started in the Deputy Secretary role in DSS on

MS WILSON: No, that's not correct. So DSS was created in - after the Coalition came to
government in 2013.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: And when the Department of Social Services was established at that point, I
was a Deputy Secretary in FaHCSIA, the previous Department. I already had responsibility for
a range of social security payments, and a number of social security - additional social
security policy areas came over from the Department of Employment into the DSS portfolio.
So I assumed responsibility for more of those at that time. Then there was a restructure, I
think in early 2014 or late 2013, where I took on all of the social security responsibilities. So it
was prior to January 2015.
MR GREGGERY: Had you ever worked at Centrelink during your long career in the Public
Service?
MS WILSON: Never.
MR GREGGERY: Right. In terms of your position as at January 2015, was there anyone with
greater policy knowledge and experience within DSS in respect of social security payments?
MS WILSON: Certainly. There were members of my staff who had worked on social security
for decades and were exceedingly expert.
MR GREGGERY: And who were they?
MS WILSON: Mr Andrew Whitecross. People at Director level. Ms Alana Foster. Mr Ian Joyce.
Who else? Let me think. They are two that stand out, and their staff, amongst my SES. I'm
trying to think of others. They would have had a number of staff in their branches who had
much longer experience and more intimate knowledge than me.
MR GREGGERY: Okay. Generally, though, were your dealings with their staff or with them,
that is, with Mr Whitecross, Ms Foster, Mr Joyce?
MS WILSON: Sorry, what was the question, Counsel?
MR GREGGERY: Were your dealings generally, in terms of people that you regarded to have
greater experience than you, with Mr Whitecross, Ms Foster and Mr Joyce or with their
staff?
MS WILSON: Usually with them, but sometimes with their staff as well. Usually my
interactions would be with them or the Group Managers that they reported through when
they weren't in Group Manager positions. So at some stages in that period, I think
Mr Whitecross would have been an Acting Group Manager and Ms Foster perhaps an Acting
Group Manager. I can't remember exactly who was acting as a Band 2 and who was a Band 1

MR GREGGERY: Alright. Can I take to you paragraph 4 of your Statement dated 21 February
2023. You describe the different attitude taken by the Coalition Government to the social
security system and the view of deserving and undeserving poor. Can you elaborate on the
concept of deserving and undeserving poor, as you understood it?
MS WILSON: There was, from my perspective, a fairly pejorative view of many jobless
people, particularly those receiving the Newstart Allowance or the Youth Allowance who
were receiving it due to being unemployed. And that was exemplified in a range of New
Policy Proposals that were agreed by the Expenditure Review Committee, particularly in the
first Coalition Budget.
MR GREGGERY: That is, the 2014 Budget?
MS WILSON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: In May 2014?
MS WILSON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: You go on to identify in that paragraph that you had built your career trying
to improve lifetime wellbeing and address the needs of disadvantaged people. What do you
mean by that?
MS WILSON: To improve outcomes for people in terms of linking them to assistance to
address barriers to employment; to address issues of financial need, either through changes
to payments or the creation of new payments or changes to eligibility for payments. I had
also been very much involved in the development of the National Disability Insurance
Scheme. I had been very much involved in a range of measures that sought to address the
needs of carers on income support. They are examples of the sorts of things that I had
worked on, I guess of which I was very proud.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. As you describe those measures, they could equally be consistent with
the duties of your role.
MS WILSON: Clearly.
MR GREGGERY: But are you saying something more than that, that it reflected work you
were passionate about or values you held deeply?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Can I take to you paragraph 8. You talk about the sequence of Ministers for
the Department of Social Security from 2015 to 2018. Is the first of those that you refer to
then Minister Morrison?

MR GREGGERY: And is the second sentence applicable to your sense of his approach?
MS WILSON: His office is what the second sentence refers to. So it was - my experience in
working with his office and then subsequent offices was that they had a lot of requests for us
of - for costings of various options that they wished to explore and data that supported that
exploration. Often those requests would come in by phone or just by email, and they would
expect a costing table or a set of data on a proposal and I would insist and put that at the
same time as that was provided we would provide some commentary on the merits of
particular proposals.
MR GREGGERY: I want to focus particularly on the period after Minister Morrison
commenced, in late December 2014, through to the Expenditure Review Committee
considering the PAYG Budget Measure on 25 March 2015. You met with Minister Morrison
on a number of occasions during that three-month period?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: When was your first meeting with him? Was it on the 30th of December
when Mr Pratt met with him at his Sydney office?
MS WILSON: I don't believe - I can't recall if I went to that meeting or not, to be honest,
Counsel. I did some preparatory work to support that meeting. I worked on Boxing Day and
in that period between Christmas and the 30th of December, but I - I can't recall if I attended
that meeting with Mr Pratt or not.
MR GREGGERY: Do you recall any feedback from Mr Pratt about the approach taken by
Minister Morrison in respect of the costings and data savings?
MS WILSON: No. No.
MR GREGGERY: Right. What is the first meeting that you recall with Minister Morrison where
these topics, to your mind - or you gained this sense from him, if at all?
MS WILSON: I - sorry, could you repeat the question?
MR GREGGERY: What is your first recollection of an interaction with Minister Morrison
where you got this sense from him, if in fact you did get it from him, as opposed to his
office?
MS WILSON: I don't believe I necessarily got it from him. It was a strong push from his office,
who I believe was speaking with his authority. But the early meetings I had with Mr Morrison
were trying to help him understand how things worked, what was on the table to be further
explored and so on. So my Statement goes to the interactions with his office.

MR GREGGERY: Were you aware or do you recall in January 2015 Mr Morrison participating
in a radio interview, 2GB I think, where there was a reference to "a tough welfare cop on the
beat" and a reference to "a crackdown"?
MS WILSON: I can't recall it, but I probably heard it at the time. But I can't recall.
MR GREGGERY: And I take it what you are conveying in paragraph 8, in the context of what
you describe in paragraph 4 about building your career in a particular way according to a
particular value set, was that the approach of the Minister's Office occasionally conflicted
with your value set?
MS WILSON: I think it - it's more that it conflicted with what I thought was the rigour of
policy development, starting with, what problem is the government seeking to fix or
address? What's the evidence about that problem? What are the merits of different
strategies that might address it? Rather than starting with a solution or a proposal that, on
occasions, appeared to me to be looking for a problem.
MR GREGGERY: We covered much of the early period in 2015 in the evidence you previously
gave.
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: We will come to some documents shortly. But broadly speaking, would you
agree that up to at least 23 January 2015, your position in respect of the proposed PAYG
measure, which was to be included in the Executive Minute to Minister Morrison, was strong
opposition on a number of grounds?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And that those grounds included both policy questions, the approach being
inconsistent with welfare policy? We can go into detail if you like, but that was one of the
grounds? I know you're nodding, but it's being - - -
MS WILSON: Yes. Sorry.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you.
MS WILSON: Beg your pardon.
MR GREGGERY: And legal grounds was another basis of your strong opposition?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you communicated your strong opposition to Ms Golightly orally?
MS WILSON: Yes.

MR GREGGERY: And you are aware now at least that it was included in documents sent
between the Departments, which Ms Golightly ultimately received?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: That is, there was no ambiguity in your position on the proposal that it
should not proceed?
MS WILSON: On the proposal as we understood it then, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. If we move forward in time to 26 February 2015. You are aware of
documents which reveal that the signed Executive Minute was sent from persons within DHS
to persons within DSS and forwarded to you on that date?
MS WILSON: Yes. I hadn't recalled that it had been forwarded to me, and I don't know
whether I read it on that day. I've since read it, immediately prior to the last hearing.
MR GREGGERY: One of the points you make in this Statement - and that paragraph can be
recalled - is that you found your interactions with Ms Golightly to be not as you might have
hoped. What do you mean when you make those references to her about how you found
your dealings with her?
MS WILSON: She was a very forceful character. She didn't enjoy being questioned and made
that pretty clear. She was very confident in her own judgment. I didn't find her to be a
collaborative and cooperative person to work with, and I had some history with Ms Golightly.
MR GREGGERY: What was that history?
MS WILSON: In 2005 she was my Deputy Secretary in the Department of Employment, and I
had a very unhappy relationship with her.
MR GREGGERY: And was she at a more senior level to you at that point?
MS WILSON: Yes. She was my direct manager.
MR GREGGERY: Right. And what period of time did that hierarchy exist between you?
MS WILSON: Not quite 12 months.
MR GREGGERY: When you say, "very unhappy", do you mean that you were lodging
complaints about her behaviour with the Secretary?
MS WILSON: No, I didn't take anything up formally.
MR GREGGERY: Was there any informal measures in respect of her management or
supervision of you?

MS WILSON: I - sorry, could you repeat the question?
MR GREGGERY: You said you didn't take anything up formally. What about informally? Were
any informal discussions had?
MS WILSON: I certainly had discussions with colleagues.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: And I was seeking other roles because I found her very difficult to work with,
and I was successful in obtaining a transfer to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet.
MR GREGGERY: Was your approach then, rather to take formal measures which were
available to you which confronted her management style, to side-step the difficulties and
look elsewhere?
MS WILSON: I did seek some assistance from peers and previous colleagues who had
experience with Ms Golightly in how to manage working with her. I didn't take it up the
hierarchy to the then Secretary. I did not pursue bullying claims against her. It's a very
fraught area in the Australian Public Service.
MR GREGGERY: Why is that?
MS WILSON: It depends upon the culture of the organisation and how well people are
supported to do that, but I didn't perceive that it would likely be successful in the
organisation for which I was working at that time and so I decided to seek roles elsewhere.
MR GREGGERY: Who was the Secretary?
MS WILSON: Mr Peter Boxall - or Dr Boxall, rather.
MR GREGGERY: What about your relationship with Finn Pratt? When you last gave evidence,
you described him, I think, in terms which might be summarised as collegiate and respectful.
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You wouldn't have any difficulty in 2015 raising with him difficulties that you
had with Ms Golightly?
MS WILSON: No. I mean, he was - he was aware of her style because they had worked
together previously, and he was aware, I believe, of other staff members in Human Services
who had not enjoyed working with her. And I guess I was trying to get on with things.
MR GREGGERY: When you say he had worked - or he worked with Ms Golightly previously,
when was that, to your knowledge?

MS WILSON: They worked together in Employment, and I believe that he was her Secretary
in the Department of Human Services when he was in the Department of Human Services,
but I'm not confident about that. I can't recall when she started in Human Services and
whether he was the Secretary then.
MR GREGGERY: To your observation in 2014 and 2015 - early 2015, did Mr Pratt and
Ms Golightly have a - the appearance of a good working relationship?
MS WILSON: I don't know that they were working together closely at that time. I don't know
that I would have had any perspectives on that in particular. I knew they went back a long
time together, having previously worked in Employment together, but I don't think I can say
more than that.
MR GREGGERY: Did you feel intimidated by Ms Golightly in 2005 when she was your Deputy
Secretary?
MS WILSON: Yes. I felt intimidated and bullied.
MR GREGGERY: And how much did your equal rank, as it were, albeit in the parent
Department, affect your perception of her?
MS WILSON: Well, we weren't a parent Department. They were two equal Departments of
State. It wasn't a parent/child relationship. In terms of our working relationship, as I say in
my Statement, it wasn't collegiate. And on a number of occasions, I felt quite pushed by her
or would experience pushback from her. And on occasions - quite often, really, if there were
a disagreement or different view between the Departments, Ms Golightly would make clear
that she believed that she spoke with the authority of her Secretary. And that was then
difficult to unpack or question her position.
MR GREGGERY: But surely you spoke with the authority of your Secretary so far as this PAYG
measure was concerned?
MS WILSON: Can you repeat the question? I'm not sure I understand what you are asking.
MR GREGGERY: I will take it in two parts. You did push back against Ms Golightly up to 23
January 2015?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And surely you spoke with the authority of Mr Pratt when you did so?
MS WILSON: Yes, I think - I believe that I had let him know my concerns about the proposal
as it was coming through at that stage and that I would let Ms Golightly know about those
concerns and pass them on, which I did. And I wanted to make sure that he wasn't blindsided
should it be escalated within DHS and raised with him by Ms Campbell. So, yes, he was
aware, and I felt that I had his support in providing feedback to DHS.

MR GREGGERY: Would you also say you had his trust in this area where you were primarily
responsible?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Complete trust?
MS WILSON: Well, I'm not sure that I can reflect on that. I think that's a question for
Mr Pratt.
MR GREGGERY: Did the existence of his trust of you appear in your day-to-day working
relationship? That is, when he questioned you about something and you gave an answer, he
accepted your position?
MS WILSON: Sometimes we would discuss it in more detail, and he would want to unpack
something a bit and understand it. But he generally, I think, accepted the advice that I put
forward.
MR GREGGERY: Well, when we come to late February in the chronology, you would agree
with me that there is no pushback by you in respect of the progression of the PAYG
measure?
MS WILSON: No, I don't agree with that. I don't accept that.
MR GREGGERY: And why don't you accept that?
MS WILSON: Because there was a discussion with Ms Golightly - and I don't know exactly
when it occurred, but we had a discussion between 26th or the 27th of February and when
the New Policy Proposal was lodged where, as I said in my second Statement, Ms Golightly
approached me, letting me know - and I now know that the Executive Minute was - came
into the Department and was forwarded to me in an email chain, which I didn't know prior to
the last hearing - that Minister Morrison wished to pursue. She came to speak with me about
that, and we discussed the nature of the proposal and, I believe, reached an agreement that
there would not be any income smoothing involved and that there would be no change to
the way that earnings were assessed, and debts were calculated for social security purposes.
And so there was pushback from me and my staff in that period of late February leading into
the Budget, which I believe resulted in the New Policy Proposal being changed.
MR GREGGERY: Apart from the insertion of those particular words, how was there to be a
change of implementation of what was proposed in the Executive Minute, to your
knowledge?
MS WILSON: Well, I didn't have a lot of knowledge about the proposed implementation, but I
believed that DHS had understood the concerns that we had raised, that they accepted our
position and that they would change, and intended to change, their implementation
approach such that it didn't require legislative change.

MR GREGGERY: You, of course, were briefed with - or copied into various drafts of the New
Policy Proposal as it went through the Budget Coordination Unit within DSS in the lead-up to
the Expenditure Review Committee?
MS WILSON: Yes, I was copied into copies as they came through.
MR GREGGERY: You were the responsible Deputy Secretary?
MS WILSON: No. I was the Deputy Secretary responsible for the social security stream.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: It was a Department of Human Services New Policy Proposal.
MR GREGGERY: But it fell within the social security stream, and it was brought forward by
Mr Pratt?
MS WILSON: It was brought forward as part of the Portfolio Budget Submission - - -
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: - - - by Minister Morrison. It's his Budget Submission.
MR GREGGERY: And the Portfolio Budget Submission is the DSS Portfolio Budget Submission?
MS WILSON: Of which a number of elements were Department of Human Services proposals
that were collated with the Portfolio Budget Submission for Minister Morrison to take
forward to the Expenditure Review Cabinet - Expenditure Review Committee, being the
Portfolio Minister in Cabinet.
MR GREGGERY: And so you had the opportunity throughout that process of some weeks to
review Exposure Drafts, Coordination Drafts and the various comments which were received
in respect of those drafts from other Departments?
MS WILSON: I had access to those. I was copied into those, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And given what you described earlier as the pushback that you were
comfortable making up to 23 January 2015 and then again on 26 or 27 January - February - - -
MS WILSON: Well, sometime between then and when the final version came in. I - as I said, I
don't recall the date.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. But you were comfortable pushing back because of your strongly held
opposition to the proposal as it was first advanced in the Executive Minute or the drafts of
the Executive Minute. You would have been interested to know what was in the New Policy
Proposal through the Exposure Draft and Coordination Draft stage, surely?

MS WILSON: Well, I was pretty consumed with my own responsibilities and the range of New
Policy Proposals that I was commissioned to take forward and have developed. I would
have - I was copied into successive versions. I was - I felt assured when I looked at the version
that was included in the Portfolio Budget Submission.
MR GREGGERY: What about on the 4th of March 2015 when you were copied into that
version of the NPP?
MS WILSON: So I believe it contained the words "there will be no change to the way in which
earnings are assessed and debts calculated" or something to that effect, and that gave me a
degree of assurance, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Now, did you make any notes of this meeting or conversation with
Ms Golightly where you say you pushed back and said, "The bottom line is this can't involve
averaging, and it has to have these words"?
MS WILSON: I don't know, because I don't have access to my personal notebooks from the
time where I would have jotted down actions to be taken. I - so I don't know.
MR GREGGERY: You don't have any emails to reflect on the conversation?
MS WILSON: No. No, I don't.
MR GREGGERY: It's an important one, though, isn't it, given the preceding position held by
you and your Department?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you're confident that those words were said by you?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: In the sense that you were pushing back on the proposal rather than
cooperating to find a way to progress it without legislative change?
MS WILSON: I believe that I was explaining what would be required as essential elements of
the proposal in a broad sense such that it didn't require legislative change so that - yes, that's
all I want to stay say.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. But your opposition to the proposal, as you understood it in January and
then in the final Executive Minute, really descended into the way in which the proposal was
implemented, which was the source of the opposition.
MS WILSON: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

MR GREGGERY: You understood the way in which the proposal was to be implemented in
January and, according to the terms of the Executive Minute - and that formed the basis of
your opposition to it.
MS WILSON: I still don't understand what you're asking me.
MR GREGGERY: Well, you say you responded to her with an expectation in broad terms
about what it could not do, but you already had knowledge of how it was proposed to be
done - - -
MS WILSON: Yes. But I believe that DHS had taken that advice on board and were changing
and had changed the proposal at the point that it was being lodged as part of the Portfolio
Budget Submission.
MR GREGGERY: And in terms of the use of PAYG data over periods where people didn't
respond to correct or confirm the accuracy of the PAYG data, what did you understand
there?
MS WILSON: I understood that there would be opportunities for customers to clarify the
information presented to them.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: And I did not - I believe that DHS had accepted our position on averaging and
smoothing, that it couldn't be used as the basis.
MR GREGGERY: You keep saying what you believed they wouldn't do. My questions are
related to what you believed they would do. Given you understood that what they would do,
as it was proposed in January and February, was contrary to your understanding of the law
and social security policy, surely you concerned yourself with what they would do?
MS WILSON: Not at a detailed level, no.
MR GREGGERY: But weren't you concerned that if nothing changed at implementation level
that you would still be in the same position?
MS WILSON: No, because I believed that DHS understood the feedback that we had provided
to them and had taken it on board. So I had no basis on which to be concerned.
MR GREGGERY: Because you believed Ms Golightly's assurance that that would be the case?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: You had no reason not to trust her?
MS WILSON: No, I didn't believe that she was a deliberately untruthful person. I found her a

MR GREGGERY: It was a simple thing, though, for you to ask, "So how will you do it if you are
not using averaging?”
MS WILSON: Well, in hindsight, yes.
MR GREGGERY: But that's what - the reason you meant, wasn't it, to work out what could
happen with what the Minister asked to be pursued?
MS WILSON: Yes. And the advice I was given was that they would be using a lot of new tools
in risk profiling and analytics to identify those people most at risk.
MR GREGGERY: That doesn't explain how debts are raised.
MS WILSON: No, but we were given assurances that debts would not be raised on a different
basis to the basis that was already the practice and supported by policy and law.
MR GREGGERY: It was a simple thing, though, for you to ask, "So how will you do it if you are
not using averaging?”
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you are saying you didn't ask the question?
MS WILSON: No.
MR GREGGERY: Despite what had led up to this point?
MS WILSON: No.
MR GREGGERY: And you say you weren't intimidated by Ms Golightly in this conversation?
MS WILSON: I - she was forceful and persuasive. I wouldn't say that I was intimidated. I
thought we had a mutual understanding.
MR GREGGERY: If it was a free-flowing conversation, as you say, it was a simple thing to ask
the question which based your opposition on multiple grounds. And I'm asking why you
didn't.
MS WILSON: I - I can't recall now all of the specifics of the conversation. It's difficult. It's a
very long time ago. But I had no reason to believe that they didn't get the DSS position. So
I - that's all I can say. In hindsight, clearly, I wish I had.
MR GREGGERY: Now, if you weren't intimidated by Ms Golightly, did you feel any pressure
from the Minister, that is, the change in approach that you describe in your third Statement?
